## Pre-Lab
1. gamma ray radiation
Well theoretically air has its own gamma absorption,
But the biggest contributor to a lower intensity is likely
the same way light intensity lowers as a matter of disntace,
because its spread farther.

So going by that
$$I_{gamma} \propto \frac 1 {x^2}$$

2. Mass attenuation solve simple equation thingy 
   
$$\mu = \rho \times \sigma$$
For 75% to come out you'd expect only 25% to travel out. so
you assume $I(x) = 0.75I_0$
$$0.75I_0 = I_0e^{-\mu x}$$
$$0.75 = e^{-\mu x}$$
$$0.75 = e^{-0.1 \times 7.874 \times x}$$

I'm going to skip all of the algebra and go straight ot the
answer
$$x = 1.7606 \ cm$$

```{python}
import warnings
from math import e, log, pi, sqrt

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import constants, odr
from scipy.stats import norm
from uncertainties import UFloat, ufloat, umath

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning, module="uncertainties")
warnings.filterwarnings(
    "ignore",
    category=FutureWarning,
    message=r"AffineScalarFunc\.__abs__\(\) is deprecated",
)
warnings.filterwarnings(
    "ignore", category=UserWarning, message="Using UFloat objects with std_dev==0"
)


def fit_odr(x: list[UFloat], y: list[UFloat], zero_intercept: bool = False):
    x_nom, x_err = [v.n for v in x], [v.s for v in x]
    y_nom, y_err = [v.n for v in y], [v.s for v in y]
    data = odr.RealData(x_nom, y_nom, sx=x_err, sy=y_err)
    if zero_intercept:
        model, beta0 = odr.Model(lambda p, x: p[0] * x), [1]
    else:
        model, beta0 = odr.Model(lambda p, x: p[0] * x + p[1]), [1, 0]
    out = odr.ODR(data, model, beta0=beta0).run()
    slope = ufloat(out.beta[0], out.sd_beta[0])
    intercept = (
        ufloat(out.beta[1], out.sd_beta[1]) if not zero_intercept else ufloat(0, 0)
    )
    y_pred = model.fcn(out.beta, np.array(x_nom))
    ss_res = np.sum((np.array(y_nom) - y_pred) ** 2)
    ss_tot = np.sum(
        np.array(y_nom) ** 2
        if zero_intercept
        else (np.array(y_nom) - np.mean(y_nom)) ** 2
    )
    r_squared = 1 - ss_res / ss_tot
    return slope, intercept, r_squared


def compsigma(a, b):
    return abs((a.n - b.n) / ((((a.s**2) + (b.s**2)) ** (1 / 2))))


def plot(
    x,
    y,
    fitodr=None,
    title="default title",
    xlabel="default xlabel",
    ylabel="default ylabel",
    show=True,
):
    if fitodr is None:
        fitodr = fit_odr(x, y)
    slope, intercept, r_squared = fitodr
    plt.figure()
    first = x[0].n
    last = x[-1].n

    plt.plot(
        [first, last],
        [first * slope.n + intercept.n, last * slope.n + intercept.n],
        "r-",
        label=f"Fit: $y = ({slope.n:.4g})x + ({intercept.n:.4g}),R^2 = {r_squared:.4f}$",
    )

    plt.errorbar(
        [v.nominal_value for v in x],
        [v.nominal_value for v in y],
        xerr=[v.std_dev for v in x],
        yerr=[v.std_dev for v in y],
        capsize=5,
        linestyle="none",
        marker="o",
        markersize=3,
        label="Data",
    )

    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel(xlabel)
    plt.ylabel(ylabel)
    plt.legend()
    if show:
        plt.show()


def plot_residuals(
    x,
    y,
    fitodr=None,
    title="Residuals",
    xlabel="default xlabel",
    ylabel="Residual (y - fit)",
    show=True,
):
    if fitodr is None:
        fitodr = fit_odr(x, y)
    slope, intercept, r_squared = fitodr
    residuals = [yi - (slope * xi + intercept) for xi, yi in zip(x, y)]
    sigma_eff = [
        sqrt(yi.std_dev**2 + (slope.n * xi.std_dev) ** 2) for xi, yi in zip(x, y)
    ]
    chi2 = sum((r.nominal_value**2) / (s**2) for r, s in zip(residuals, sigma_eff))
    dof = len(y) - 1
    chi2_reduced = chi2 / dof
    zero_fit = (
        ufloat(0, 0),
        ufloat(0, 0),
        0.0,
    )  # was None — plot()'s label needs a float

    plot(
        x,
        residuals,
        fitodr=zero_fit,
        title=f"{title} ($\\chi^2_\\nu = {chi2_reduced:.3f}$)",
        xlabel=xlabel,
        ylabel=ylabel,
        show=show,
    )

    return chi2_reduced


def two_tailed_p(diff: float):
    z = abs(diff)
    return 2 * norm.sf(z)


```

## Experiment 1

### Aim

The aim of this experiment is to experimentally deduce
the linear absorption coefficient $\mu$ of a miscellaneous
barrier.

### Method

First is measuring. We used pvc plastic as our barrier, for
all three barriers we measured precisely using a calliper.
Me and my lab partner both did independent measurements.
This is for our own error propagation.

Then we set up our equipment, with a stand, we clamped the
geiger counter connected to the lab computer above the lead
uncasing. We do not move or touch the position of this
geiger counter for all until the next experiment.

We then used 2 minute time intervals to measure the
background radiation. we use 2 minute intervals for all
measurements. We use seconds as our increments.

After measuring background radiation we chose barium as our
radioactive substance, due to its high half life and its
reasonably high activity. We inserted it into the lead
casing. We recorded the intensity using the same 2 minute
interval, and repeated the process with 1 and 2 layers of
the same thickness pvc barrier.

The software we were using, vernier had a statistics tab,
which had both a mean and a standard deviation, we recorded
those only.

Since our results were bad, we attempted this again, but
instead we started with three barriers of pvc plastic, and
situated the geiger as close as possible to the plastic,
putting our geiger close to the substance increases our
radiation, which yields better results. We repeated the
entire experiment with this closer situated geiger

Also for our first experiment we only had 2 pvc barriers,
whereas the second embettered experiment had 3 pvc barriers.

### Conclusions

I have created two functions for the purpose of data
interpolation. They are very functional coated in the way
that they operate and I will explain them wordily.

Firstly the tuples such that its of size two and the second
value in each tuple is just the ufloat, since ufloat does
the error propagation for me.

Then I combine the data based on if its one layer and sum
them. So for example I sum all of the 1 pvc layer
datapoints. This is automatically error propagated because
of ufloats.

I sort this and then remove the background from each value.


```{python}
# Functions not created with ai btw
def databetter(data: list[tuple[int, float, float]]):
    ufloats = [(x[0], ufloat(x[1], x[2] / sqrt(120))) for x in data]
    numbers = set([x[0] for x in ufloats])
    combinedufloats = [list(filter(lambda y: y[0] == x, ufloats)) for x in numbers]
    values = [(x[0][0], sum([y[1] for y in x]) / len(x)) for x in combinedufloats]
    sortedvalues = sorted(values, key=lambda x: x[0])
    out = [(x[0], x[1] - sortedvalues[0][1]) for x in sortedvalues[1:]]
    return out
```

Next one is just some math
$$I_0e^{-\mu x} = I_n$$
$$-\mu x = \ln{\frac{I_n} {I_0}}$$
and we use $y = \ln{\frac{I_n} {I_0}}$ and 
$x = -x$
This is what our next function does, it fits a linear
regression line of it and returns the line pretty much.

```{python}
def datainterpolate(data: list[tuple]):
    xdata = [-x[0] * lengthpvc for x in data[1:]]
    ydata = [umath.log(x[1] / data[0][1]) for x in data[1:]]
    out = fit_odr(xdata, ydata)
    return out
```

We can now use these functions to interpolate the data

Barium is in the area of 400KeV gamma radiation. And this
corresponds to, assuming pvc plastic is 1.4$\frac g {cm^3}$.
is 14.

I know i'm not sourcing but one source listed pvc plastic as
1.35 ~ 1.45 g/cm^3 so we are using 0.05 as some uncertainty
here.

This just corresponds to a $\mu$ of $14\pm0.5 m^{-1}$

So we compare the sigma value of this to our value.

```{python}
mu2 = datainterpolate(databetter(exp2data))[0]
print(compsigma(mu2, ufloat(14, 0.5)))
```

And we get $<3$ sigma, So success on our second experiment,
our second experiment is consistent with the real expected
value.


unfortunately, for our first experiment, where we had the
geiger situated farther away, with only 2 pvc layers, we get
a value of:

```{python}
mu1 = datainterpolate(databetter(exp1data))[0]
print(compsigma(mu1, ufloat(1.4, 0.05)*10))
```

This is significantly larger than 3, and indicates a large
systematic error in our experiment. The reasons why are
likely due to how much background radiation actually matters
when you increase the distance of the geiger to the
radioactive matter. Luck becomes a huge factor and the noise
of the background radiation starts outweighing the
radioactive matter by large magnitudes.
